title: SMTP Service Extension for Returning Enhanced Error Codes
summary: Defines an SMTP extension so servers can add enhanced status codes to their replies, giving clearer and more machine-readable reasons for success or failure of mail delivery.

plainLanguage.summary: When a letter cannot be delivered, the post office sends back a code that tells you exactly why, not just that it failed.

questions: what are smtp enhanced status codes
how do smtp enhanced status codes work
what is the format of an smtp enhanced status code
subtitle: Lets an SMTP server put machine-readable status codes like 5.1.1 in front of its reply text.

tldr.problem: SMTP servers explain failures in free text that varies from server to server and language to language, which makes automatic delivery failure reports hard to build.
tldr.mechanism: A server that advertises the ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES extension starts the text of its 2xx, 4xx and 5xx replies with a status code from RFC 1893, such as 5.1.1.
tldr.outcome: Clients and mail systems get a coded reason they can translate into any language and put into delivery status notifications.

today: RFC 2034 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES extension and relies on RFC 1893 for the codes themselves.

sections.title: Why SMTP Needed Enhanced Codes
sections.content:
This memo defines an extension to SMTP in which a server adds the enhanced mail system status codes of RFC 1893 to its replies. The text of an SMTP reply is meant for people and differs between servers. The RFC points to the needs of a modern, international, multilingual Internet, where error conditions should have codes that can be translated into different languages.

RFC 1894 defines delivery status notifications that carry such coded material to users. But the program that builds one is often reacting to an error it received from a remote SMTP server. So remote servers need a way to embed the codes in their replies and a way to tell a client that they are doing so. The extension uses the mechanism of RFC 1869 to do that.
sections.plainLanguage: Words in an error message change from place to place. A short code does not, so everyone can understand why the mail failed.

sections.title: The Extension Framework
sections.content:
The RFC lays the extension out as a short list. The service extension is named Enhanced-Status-Codes, and the EHLO keyword is ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES. The keyword takes no parameter, and the extension defines no new SMTP verbs.

What it does change is the reply text. In all 2xx, 4xx and 5xx replies, other than the initial greeting and any response to HELO or EHLO, the text is prefaced with a status code as defined in RFC 1893. The code is always followed by one or more spaces.
sections.plainLanguage: A server says a special word to announce that it adds codes. After that, every success or failure message starts with its code.

sections.title: Where the Codes Go and What They Look Like
sections.content:
A status code has three numbers separated by dots: a class, a subject and a detail. The ABNF is status-code ::= class "." subject "." detail, where the class is 2, 4 or 5 and the subject and detail are each one to three digits.

The codes must agree with the primary reply code. A 2xx reply carries a 2.X.X code, a 4xx reply a 4.X.X code and a 5xx reply a 5.X.X code. Intermediate 3xx replies are not included. When a reply spans several lines, the same status code must appear at the start of the text on every line.

Servers supporting the extension must attach the codes whether or not the client used EHLO.
sections.plainLanguage: The code is like a label with a number, a topic and a detail, and its first number must match whether things went well, need a retry, or failed for good.

sections.title: No Client Opt-In
sections.content:
Most SMTP extensions only change server behavior after the client asks. This one does not. The specification gives clients no way to ask for the codes or to refuse them, and a compliant server includes them regardless of what the client expects.

The RFC says this omission is entirely intentional. Because of the generally poor state of SMTP server error code implementation, any step toward more comprehensible error codes should benefit all clients, extended or not.

The RFC stresses that this is a very special case. It MUST NOT be taken as a license for future SMTP extensions to dramatically change SMTP client-server interaction without server announcement and a corresponding enabling command from the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually you have to ask for extras. Here the server gives the codes to everyone, because clearer errors are good for everybody.

sections.title: A Worked Dialogue
sections.content:
The RFC shows a session. After EHLO the server advertises ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES. The MAIL command gets 250 2.1.0 and the first recipient 250 2.1.5. A second recipient gets 550 5.1.1 Mailbox "nosuchuser" does not exist. A third gets a two-line 551 reply with 5.7.1 on both lines. The accepted message gets 250 2.6.0 and QUIT gets 221 2.0.0.

The RFC then shows a nondelivery notification a client might build from this. The per-recipient Status: fields hold the codes, such as 5.1.1 for a bad destination mailbox address. The example notes that the reporting MTA omitted the enhanced codes from its diagnostic-code fields to reduce clutter.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows a mail run where one address is fine and two are not. Each answer carries a code, and the bounce message turns them into plain reasons.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The only concern raised is that extra detail in server replies gives away extra information about the server. The RFC notes that such information could conceivably help someone get around server security. The benefit of providing more detail must always be weighed against the security implications of doing so.
sections.plainLanguage: The more a server says about why it said no, the more a sneaky person learns, so servers should think about how much to tell.
